subject: ESL
label: ESL level E3
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in ESL level E3 English as a second language, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 11 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Plans and future
modules.outcome: use going to and will to talk about plans
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Plans and future', taught in a way that is short, spoken, with pictures and real objects. The target is clear: use going to and will to talk about plans. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Plans and future' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: use going to and will to talk about plans, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow. I will call you tonight.' Going to for plans, will for decisions now. Method: Model run for 'Plans and future'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 15 to 25 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a voice note or one page of work.
modules.standard: Use going to and will to talk about plans: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, Choose going to for plans already decided. Model: "I'm going to visit my cousin next week." Form: be plus going to plus the base verb. Reason: the plan was made before the moment of speaking.

Step 2, Choose will for sudden decisions and predictions. Model: "It's cold. I'll close the window." "I think it will rain tomorrow." Reason: the decision happens now, and a prediction is an opinion about the future.
Step 3, Make negatives and questions. Model: "I'm not going to work this weekend." "Are you going to study tonight?" "She won't come." Reason: won't is will not, and the main verb stays plain.

Step 4, Compare in one sentence. "I'm going to study medicine; I think I'll enjoy it." Reason: the plan uses going to, the guess about enjoying uses will. Time words: tomorrow, next year, in two weeks, soon.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Tomorrow I will to go to the market." Right: "Tomorrow I will go to the market." Another wrong: "I going to eat." Right: "I'm going to eat." Never omit the form of be.
Step 6, Ask about plans. A: "What are you going to do this summer?" B: "I'm going to visit my grandparents, and I'll help on the farm." A: "That sounds great. I think you'll enjoy it."

Step 7, Your turn. Write three sentences: a plan, a prediction and a sudden decision. Model answer: "I'm going to start a sports club. I think it will be popular. Oh, the phone is ringing; I'll answer it."

modules.title: Travel and holidays
modules.outcome: describe a trip and book tickets
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Travel and holidays', taught in a way that is short, spoken, with pictures and real objects. The target is clear: describe a trip and book tickets. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Travel and holidays' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: describe a trip and book tickets, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'I would like a ticket to Dubai, please. What time does the train leave? Is it direct?' Method: Model run for 'Travel and holidays'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 15 to 25 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a voice note or one page of work.
modules.standard: Describe a trip and book tickets: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, Describe a trip in the past simple with details. Model: "Last July we travelled to the coast by train. The journey took four hours. We stayed in a small hotel near the beach." Reason: the past simple tells the story.
Step 2, Add feeling and description. "The sea was clear and warm. The food was delicious, but the town was crowded." Reason: adjectives make a trip description specific, and "but" shows contrast.

Step 3, Book a ticket politely. Customer: "I'd like two return tickets to Kandy, please." Clerk: "When are you travelling?" Customer: "Next Saturday, in the morning." Reason: "return" means there and back; "single" means one way.
Step 4, Ask about times and prices. "What time does the train leave?" "How long does the journey take?" "Is there a seat by the window?" Reason: present simple questions are used for timetables.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "I want two ticket to Kandy." Right: "I'd like two tickets to Kandy." Another error: "We have gone to the coast last July." Right: "We went to the coast last July."
Step 6, Write a short postcard. "Dear Maya, We are having a great time at the coast. The weather is sunny, and we swim every day. Tomorrow we are going to visit a fort. See you soon, Imran."

Step 7, Your turn. Write a three-line dialogue booking one single bus ticket to the capital for tomorrow. Model answer: "I'd like a single ticket to the capital, please." "For which day?" "Tomorrow morning, please."

modules.title: Opinions and reasons
modules.outcome: give opinions with because and so
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Opinions and reasons', taught in a way that is short, spoken, with pictures and real objects. The target is clear: give opinions with because and so. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Opinions and reasons' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: give opinions with because and so, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'I think homework is useful because it helps me practise. However, too much is tiring.' Opinion, reason, other side. Method: Model run for 'Opinions and reasons'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 15 to 25 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a voice note or one page of work.
modules.standard: Give opinions with because and so: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, State your opinion with a fixed phrase. Model: "In my opinion, students should wear uniform." Alternatives: "I think that", "I believe that", "As far as I'm concerned". Reason: a phrase shows that you are giving a view, not a fact.
Step 2, Give a reason with because. "I think students should wear uniform because it makes everyone equal." Reason: because answers the question why, and the reason follows it directly.
Step 3, Give a result with so. "Uniforms are cheap, so families save money." Reason: "so" shows the result, while "because" shows the cause. Compare: "Families save money because uniforms are cheap."
Step 4, Agree and disagree politely. "I agree with you." "I see your point, but I think it is too strict." Reason: starting with "I see your point" keeps the tone respectful.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Because it is cheap, so I like it." Right: "I like it because it is cheap" or "It is cheap, so I like it." Never use both because and so in one clause.
Step 6, Build a mini-paragraph. "I think homework is useful because it helps us remember. It also builds a habit, so we study better. However, too much homework is tiring."

Step 7, Your turn. Give your opinion on school lunch with one because and one so. Model answer: "I think school should serve hot lunch because students learn better when they are not hungry. It is healthy, so parents are happy too."

modules.title: Emails and notes
modules.outcome: write a short email and note
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Emails and notes', taught in a way that is short, spoken, with pictures and real objects. The target is clear: write a short email and note. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Emails and notes' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: write a short email and note, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Subject: Football practice. Dear Coach, I cannot come on Friday because I am ill. Best wishes, Omar. Method: Model run for 'Emails and notes'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 15 to 25 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a voice note or one page of work.
modules.standard: Write a short email and note: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, Plan an email with four parts: greeting, reason for writing, details, closing. Reason: a plan lets the reader find the key information quickly.

Step 2, Write a friendly email. "Hi Nadia, Thanks for your message. I'm writing to ask about Saturday. Are you free at three? Let me know. Best wishes, Hamid." Use contractions for friends, and "Dear" for a teacher.

Step 3, Write a formal email with polite phrases. "Dear Mr Silva, I am writing to ask whether I can borrow a book from the library. I would be grateful for your reply. Yours sincerely, Hamid." Reason: formal emails avoid contractions.

Step 4, Write a short note. "Mum, I've gone to Ravi's house to study. I'll be back at six. Don't wait for dinner. Love, Hamid." Reason: a note is short, gives the key facts, and uses no long greeting.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "Dear Sir, i want the book now." Right: "Dear Sir, I would like to borrow the book, please." Capital I, polite request, and a complete sentence make the email correct.
Step 6, Correct the closing. For a name you know: "Best wishes" or "Kind regards". For a teacher: "Yours sincerely" if you know the name. Reason: closings show how formal the email is.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a three-sentence email to a friend inviting him to your birthday on Sunday at five. Model answer: "Hi Sam, I'm having a birthday party on Sunday at five. Can you come? Please tell me by Friday. Best wishes, Hamid."

modules.standard: Follow a short classroom explanation: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, Listen for the main idea first. Teacher: "Today we'll learn how plants make food. Leaves use sunlight, water and air." Main idea: how plants make food. Reason: you find the topic before the details.
Step 2, Spot signpost words. "First", "next", "so", "for example" and "in conclusion" tell you how ideas link. Model note: "First: roots take in water." Reason: signposts help you order the notes.
Step 3, Take brief notes. Teacher: "Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and sunlight gives them energy." Note: "leaves - CO2 + light = energy." Reason: notes need keywords only.

Step 4, Ask a clarifying question politely. "Sorry, could you explain what photosynthesis means?" or "Could you repeat the second point, please?" Reason: you ask about words you missed, not the whole lesson.
Step 5, Fix an error. A student writes: "Plants make light." The teacher said: "Plants use light to make food." Check the verb. Corrected note: "plants use light to make food."

Step 6, Summarise in two sentences. "The teacher explained how plants make food. They use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and they produce sugar and oxygen." Reason: a summary has the main idea plus the key detail.

Step 7, Your turn. Teacher says: "The water cycle has three steps. Water evaporates, it condenses into clouds, and it falls as rain." Write notes and one summary sentence. Model answer: "water cycle: evaporate - condense - rain." "Water rises, makes clouds, and falls as rain."

modules.standard: Present and answer questions: at least 4 of 5 attempts understood by a listener who does not know you.
steps: Step 1, Plan a talk with a hook, three points and a close. Topic: "A day without phones". Hook: "Imagine one whole day without your phone." Reason: a hook gains attention.

Step 2, Write each point with a reason. "First, we would talk more with our family. Second, we would sleep better, because there's no screen at night. Finally, we would read more." Reason: first, second and finally make the structure obvious.
Step 3, Add a counter-view. "Some people say they need phones for safety. That's true, but we can use them only for calls." Reason: showing you know another view makes your opinion stronger.

Step 4, Practise answering questions. Q: "Would you really do it?" A: "Yes, I think I would, but only for one day." Q: "Why?" A: "Because I want to see if I can." Reason: answers start with a direct response, then a reason.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "If I will have no phone, I sleep more." Right: "If I had no phone, I would sleep more." Or simple: "If I have no phone, I'll sleep more." Match the tenses in both clauses.

Step 6, Close the talk clearly. "To sum up, a day without phones would improve my family time, my sleep and my reading. Thank you. I'm happy to answer questions." Reason: "to sum up" signals the ending.

Step 7, Your turn. Write the hook and the close for a talk on "Why I like my town". Model answer: "Hook: What makes a town feel like home?" "Close: To sum up, my town is friendly, safe and green. Thank you. Any questions?"
